title: The List

jokes.text: Changing the Marines' slogan to 'I think sarge likes me.'
jokes.setup: The debate over lifting the ban on gays in the military — the Marines would change their slogan from 'looking for a few good men'
jokes.punchline: 'I think sarge likes me' — a nervous, in-group gay panic joke delivered as if the fear itself is the absurdity
jokes.explanation: Competent late-night monologue joke of its era. The structure is clean — familiar slogan subverted with paranoid inner monologue — but the premise leans on gay-panic tropes rather than genuine wit. Gets the job done as a topical opener.

dialogue.line: They will be changing their slogan from 'The marines are looking for a few good men' to... 'I think sarge likes me.'

jokes.text: Will they edit Klinger out of M*A*S*H episodes if they enforce the gay ban?
jokes.setup: Confusion over how the military would enforce a gay ban
jokes.punchline: Klinger (a man who cross-dressed to get out of the Army) becomes the absurd test case — will they retroactively censor pop culture?
jokes.explanation: A sharper extension of the previous joke — moves from predictable slogan subversion to an absurdist hypothetical (retroactive pop-culture editing) that has more comic legs. The Klinger reference is culturally specific in a satisfying way.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Will they take the M.A.S.H episodes and edit out Klinger?

jokes.text: 'Here comes one with no segue.' — Larry openly announcing his awkward transition to the prom bit
jokes.setup: Standard late-night monologue; topics are expected to flow with some connective tissue
jokes.punchline: Larry abandons the pretense entirely and flags his own lack of transition as a self-aware joke
jokes.explanation: This is a sharp piece of meta-comedy that works both as a late-night bit and as a character note — Larry's self-awareness about the mechanics of his own show. Economy is excellent: four words do all the work. Feels very Larry Sanders in its wry self-deprecation.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The schools have switched to the more formal, prettier, carnation-covered metal detectors.

jokes.text: Schools switching to 'carnation-covered metal detectors' for prom
jokes.setup: Prom time across America; schools are going formal and pretty
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of floral decoration and metal detectors — school violence dressed up in prom finery
jokes.explanation: The best monologue joke in the cold open. 'Carnation-covered metal detectors' is a genuinely elegant image — the collision of innocence (carnations, prom) with violence (metal detectors) compressed into a single noun phrase. The economy is excellent: the punchline is five words that paint a complete, absurd picture.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Do not flip around. No flipping.

jokes.text: 'And Conan O'Brien thinks this will be easy.' — Larry's cutting aside about his competition
jokes.setup: End of monologue; the jokes have been functional but not spectacular
jokes.punchline: Larry implies Conan (a real late-night rival, newly launched) overestimates the job — a competitive dig dressed as casual commentary
jokes.explanation: Clever meta-layer: the Larry Sanders Show exists in a real TV landscape, so namedropping Conan as a rival blurs fiction and reality in a way that rewards attentive viewers. Strong character integration — Larry's insecurity about competition is a defining trait. The rewatch bonus comes from knowing how the rivalry plays out in the series.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I slept with Francine last night.

jokes.text: 'Do not flip around. No flipping.' — Hank's desperate, increasingly pathetic iteration of Larry's sign-off
jokes.setup: Larry says 'Don't flip around' as a standard audience sign-off
jokes.punchline: Hank's variation 'No flipping' is the kind of desperate, self-important co-host addition that shows he thinks he's adding something while actually diminishing himself
jokes.explanation: A compact character joke: Hank can't help himself from adding his own spin to Larry's bit, but his contribution is a nothing-phrase that only underscores how little he brings. 'No flipping' is the sad echo of 'Don't flip around' — same idea, less authority. Pure Hank Kingsley energy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It was the entire weekend.

jokes.text: Artie's post-show ritual of blame-deflection: 'The audience was shit, huh? The sound was no good? It's too hot in here? The show was fine.'
jokes.setup: Larry comes offstage looking troubled; Artie preemptively cycles through every excuse Larry might use
jokes.punchline: Having listed all possible deflections, Artie simply declares 'The show was fine' — shutting down Larry's impending spiral before it starts
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. Artie's preemptive list of excuses reveals two things simultaneously: he knows Larry's patterns cold, and he's seen this exact scene play out dozens of times. The structure (rapid list → blunt declaration) is crisp. High character integration — this is textbook Artie managing Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That woman smashed your People's Choice Award. Why take it out on the award? The fucking people gave you that award.

jokes.text: Artie cataloguing his own drunk ex-wife visits: 'I've knocked on ex-wives' doors when I was tanked up and horny. God bless those four ladies.'
jokes.setup: Larry confesses he slept with Francine; Artie tries to find an excuse ('You were drunk, right?')
jokes.punchline: Artie's aside about his own four ex-wives — delivered with affectionate nostalgia — is a dark self-revelation that normalizes his chaos while inadvertently dwarfing Larry's problem
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn's Artie in a nutshell: debauched, self-aware, weirdly wise. 'God bless those four ladies' does enormous work — it's affectionate, dark, and reveals a man with a trail of wreckage he's made peace with. The number 'four' is the precision that makes it land. Strong character integration: only Artie could say this.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Big mistake. Big, big mistake.

jokes.text: 'That woman smashed your People's Choice Award... Why take it out on the award? The fucking people gave you that award.'
jokes.setup: Artie is alarmed Larry slept with Francine again, recounting how destructive she is
jokes.punchline: Artie's moral outrage is directed not at the relationship damage but at the disrespect shown to the People's Choice Award — a hilariously misplaced priority that also subtly mocks the award's prestige
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structural misdirection is clean: we expect Artie to object to the relationship itself, but his fury lands entirely on the award. 'The fucking people gave you that award' is a genuine line — it sounds like sincere outrage while being absurd. The joke is that a showbiz lifer like Artie has oddly specific respect for the People's Choice Award, a notoriously uncool honor. Excellent quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: He's gayer than a French horn.

jokes.text: Artie whispers 'Big mistake. Big, big mistake.' as Larry goes back on stage
jokes.setup: Larry is about to go back on air despite Artie's alarm about the Francine situation
jokes.punchline: Artie's repeated 'big, big mistake' — gravely intoned — becomes both a sincere warning and a comic mantra
jokes.explanation: Establishes the episode's running gag. The repetition of 'big, big mistake' is doing structural work — it will pay off in callbacks later. On its own it's a solid character beat; as a setup for the running gag it earns a rewatch bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: I had sex with him. Will that be a problem for you?

jokes.text: 'He's gay, you know.' / 'He is not gay.' / 'He's gayer than a French horn.' / 'I had sex with him.'
jokes.setup: Francine casually declares Alec Baldwin is gay; Larry dismisses it
jokes.punchline: The escalation through 'He's gayer than a French horn' peaks with Francine's flat, devastating 'I had sex with him' — which simultaneously proves he's not gay AND reveals their affair in one sentence
jokes.explanation: Exceptional comedic construction. 'He's gayer than a French horn' is a wonderfully specific, absurdist simile — French horns have no inherent gayness, which is exactly why it's funny. Then the punchline does double duty: it refutes her gay claim while simultaneously revealing the affair. The information delivery is perfectly efficient. This is genuinely skilled joke architecture.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: Ask if the Saab's clutch is still sticking.

jokes.text: 'Ask if the Saab's clutch is still sticking.' — Larry's request to Francine about asking Alec Baldwin
jokes.setup: Larry has just learned Francine slept with Alec Baldwin; he's trying to be cool about it
jokes.punchline: The weird specificity of the Saab clutch question — Larry clearly knows intimate details of Baldwin's life from Francine — reveals how deep the wound goes while Larry performs nonchalance
jokes.explanation: A beautifully layered character joke. Larry's knowledge of Baldwin's Saab suggests he's been obsessing about this relationship far more than he's admitting. The specificity (not just 'his car' but 'the Saab's clutch') does the comic and dramatic work simultaneously. Very Larry Sanders.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: When you eat at Hank's, you and your food... are going... on an adventure.

jokes.text: Hank pitching his rotating restaurant 'Hank's Look-Around Cafe' — 'When you eat at Hank's, you and your food... are going on an adventure.'
jokes.setup: Hank is reading notes from his business manager about why the rotating restaurant is financially unviable
jokes.punchline: Hank's grandiose pitch for a street-level rotating restaurant, delivered with messianic conviction — 'you and your food are going on an adventure' — is pure delusional showbiz ego
jokes.explanation: Classic Hank delusion comedy. The rotating restaurant is an inherently absurd idea; the business manager's note that it's at street level (so there's no view, defeating the whole purpose) is devastating. Hank's response — 'you and your food are going on an adventure' — is a masterpiece of self-important non-logic. High character integration: only Hank believes this sentence is a complete answer to the criticism.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: So I'd like you to take your opinion and shove it right up your ass. Regards, Hank Kingsley. Fax that back to him.

jokes.text: Hank's response to criticism of the rotating floor: 'Forget the rotating floor?' — delivered with wounded disbelief
jokes.setup: The practical suggestion: just open the restaurant without the rotating floor
jokes.punchline: For Hank, the rotating floor IS the restaurant — the idea of separating them is incomprehensible. His tone treats it like someone suggested removing the Eiffel Tower from Paris.
jokes.explanation: A solid character reaction beat — it's three words that contain multitudes about Hank's delusion. The comedy is entirely in the delivery and the implicit absurdity of his attachment to an impractical gimmick.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Get Chuck Woolery on the phone.

jokes.text: 'I am on a first-name basis with some of the most influential, some of the most powerful people in this business. So... get Chuck Woolery on the phone.'
jokes.setup: Hank builds to what we expect will be a powerful Hollywood name
jokes.punchline: Chuck Woolery — the game-show host, far from the power brokers Hank implied — lands as the funniest possible deflation of Hank's self-mythology
jokes.explanation: The best Hank joke in the episode and one of the best in the transcript overall. The setup is a slow, grandiose build — 'most influential, most powerful' — that promises a major name. Chuck Woolery is the perfect anti-climax: not nobody, but emphatically not the room Hank claimed. The specific choice of Woolery (a dated game-show host with an industry-insider recognizability) is exactly right. Structure is near-flawless: long windup, perfectly timed beat, single devastating name. This is what 8+ comedy looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: These Baldwin boys seem to be multiplying like fucking jackrabbits.

jokes.text: 'These Baldwin boys seem to be multiplying like fucking jackrabbits.'
jokes.setup: The booker explains they canceled Alec because Arsenio had Billy Baldwin and Leno had Stephen Baldwin — too many Baldwins on TV at once
jokes.punchline: Artie's colorful summation captures the absurdity of the Baldwin sibling saturation of 1993 television
jokes.explanation: A well-delivered Artie line with good economy. The 'jackrabbits' simile is vivid and appropriately profane for the character. Works as observational comedy about early-90s Hollywood and as character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: What's he play with? With his ass, I suppose.

jokes.text: 'A man with no arms playing the piano. True triumph of the spirit.' / 'What's he play with?' / 'With his ass, I suppose.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks who the replacement guest is; the booker describes a feel-good human-interest act
jokes.punchline: Artie's flat 'With his ass, I suppose' — delivered as a genuine guess, not malice — turns the inspirational segment into something uncomfortable and funny
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — the whole exchange takes four lines and lands with precision. 'With his ass, I suppose' has the perfect deadpan Artie quality: he's not being cruel, he's genuinely solving a logical problem. The callback of this joke later (when someone says 'I thought he used something else') adds rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Remember what happened with all those Carradines?

jokes.text: Artie's escalating graphic description of what Larry will picture during the interview: '...you blink, and you see him screwing your lovely Francine. You see her face. You see his face slobbering in her ear. You see legs all entangled. You hear the grunts.'
jokes.setup: Artie is warning Larry that interviewing Alec Baldwin (who slept with Francine) is a bad idea
jokes.punchline: What starts as a reasonable warning escalates into graphic, cinematic detail — Artie paints the scene with the granularity of a film director, making it much worse than any warning needed to be
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest sustained comedy moments. The escalation follows a perfect arc: professional concern → visual description → pornographic detail. 'Slobbering in her ear' is the peak — specific, gross, and clearly a detail Artie has visualized himself, which makes it funnier. Also plants the seed that pays off in the break scene where Larry admits 'she was on top.'

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I saw them together at a rolling disco party a few years ago.

jokes.text: 'If I cancel, don't I look like a jerk?' / 'No. Paula looks like a jerk.'
jokes.setup: Larry worries about his image if he cancels Alec Baldwin
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately deflects the reputational hit to Paula (the booker) — a completely practical, amoral solution delivered as obvious wisdom
jokes.explanation: Crisp two-line exchange that says everything about showbiz culture in eight words. Artie's answer isn't even cynical — it's just practical. The comedy comes from how casually he throws Paula under the bus as a solution. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You see his face slobbering in her ear. You see legs all entangled. You hear the grunts.

jokes.text: 'Big mistake. Big, big mistake.' — Artie repeats his mantra as Larry flip-flops on canceling Baldwin
jokes.setup: Larry keeps changing his mind about Baldwin; Artie keeps giving the same verdict
jokes.punchline: The repetition of the exact same line — 'big, big mistake' — grows funnier with each iteration as Artie's fatalism proves increasingly correct
jokes.explanation: The running gag is now paying dividends. Artie saying 'big, big mistake' while Larry books/cancels/books Baldwin is a structural comedy device that earns laughs through repetition and the inevitability of being proven right.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No. Paula looks like a jerk.

jokes.text: Beverly's excited 'Hi, I'm Beverly!' to Alec Baldwin in the pre-show greenroom — wide-eyed starstruck sincerity amid Larry's neurotic spiral
jokes.setup: Larry is on edge about Baldwin arriving; introductions are made in the hallway
jokes.punchline: Beverly's guileless enthusiasm is a tonal non-sequitur that punctures Larry's anxiety — she introduces herself as if it's the best day of her life
jokes.explanation: A small but genuine laugh — Beverly's total obliviousness to the tension in the room is a good tonal counterpoint. Not a major joke but earns its moment.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: A little chocolate never hurt anybody.

jokes.text: 'That girl Darlene — did she work on Knots Landing?' / 'She worked at Knott's Berry Farm for a short time.'
jokes.setup: Baldwin asks if one of Larry's staff worked on Knots Landing (the TV show)
jokes.punchline: Larry's response pivots to Knott's Berry Farm (the amusement park) — an inadvertent near-homophone that deflates Baldwin's implication about his conquests
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever wordplay joke — the Knots Landing / Knott's Berry Farm confusion isn't telegraphed, and it works on multiple levels (the absurd deflation of celebrity gossip onto theme park employment). The best wordplay moment in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: I thought he used something else.

jokes.text: Larry's increasingly manic assertion that everything is fine with Baldwin dating Francine: 'Be my guest... Couldn't be better. Thrilled you're here. Fantastic. Don't worry about it.'
jokes.setup: Baldwin asks if Larry has a problem with him having dated Francine post-divorce
jokes.punchline: Larry's over-reassurance — cascading affirmations that escalate in desperate cheerfulness — is a perfect portrait of a man who is absolutely not fine
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe comedy. Each successive 'it's fine' makes it more obvious it isn't. The accumulation of reassurances ('Couldn't be better. Thrilled you're here. Fantastic.') is a precise comedy escalation — each word more hollow than the last. Larry Sanders at its most painfully relatable.

dialogue.line: She worked at Knott's Berry Farm for a short time.

jokes.text: Baldwin casually describing Francine as 'a little flaky' to her ex-husband, then 'I see why you'd want out.' / Larry: 'Yeah, you bet.'
jokes.setup: Baldwin reminisces warmly about Francine, then casually critiques her
jokes.punchline: Baldwin's easy dismissal of Francine puts Larry in the impossible position of agreeing with a man who slept with his ex-wife. Larry's 'Yeah, you bet' is the sound of a man drowning with a smile.
jokes.explanation: Strong cringe beat. Baldwin's breezy 'I see why you'd want out' forces Larry to validate his ex-wife's new lover's assessment of her — and he does it instantly, compulsively. 'Yeah, you bet' is the perfect Larry capitulation.

dialogue.speaker: Alec
dialogue.line: We had some really, really wild times together. Of course, that was back in crazier days.

jokes.text: Alec Baldwin staying for the whole show after the audience applauds — 'The people have spoken.' / 'Some of the people have spoken.'
jokes.setup: Baldwin asks if he can stay; scattered applause from the audience grants permission
jokes.punchline: Larry's instant walk-back — 'Some of the people have spoken' — undercuts the democratic sentiment with precision; a few claps does not a mandate make
jokes.explanation: Efficient and smart. The immediate self-correction deflates the artificial enthusiasm of TV audience moments. Very much in the show's mock-sincere register.

dialogue.speaker: Alec
dialogue.line: She's a little flaky. I see why you'd want out.

jokes.text: On air, Larry begins 'You and I have something in common...' and the audience assumes he means Francine — Larry leans in, then reveals it's Multiple Sclerosis charity work
jokes.setup: Baldwin says on air 'you and I have something in common' — the studio audience whooos, anticipating the Francine reveal
jokes.punchline: Baldwin clarifies it's the MS charity work. Larry: 'I know. I know. That, too.' — having already broadcast the affair to the audience
jokes.explanation: Superb structural comedy. The episode has carefully seeded both the MS charity meeting and the Francine revelation — here both threads collide on air. The audience's whoo is funnier than any punchline could be. Larry's 'I know. I know. That, too.' is perfectly calibrated self-awareness — he knows he jumped the gun but owns it. This is the episode's comedy engine firing on all cylinders.

dialogue.line: The phrase 'Be my guest' comes to mind.

jokes.text: In the commercial break, Larry admits: 'From the time he walked out, all I saw was him fucking her. And she was on top. That lazy bastard.'
jokes.setup: Artie's earlier graphic description planted the image; Larry now confirms it took hold during the live interview
jokes.punchline: 'That lazy bastard' — Larry's specific detail (she was on top) reveals he's been obsessing over the sexual mechanics of Francine and Baldwin, and his outrage has landed on Baldwin's passivity
jokes.explanation: Outstanding character comedy and callback payoff. Artie's earlier graphic description prepared us for Larry's spiral, but 'she was on top / that lazy bastard' is a punchline nobody could have predicted. Larry's jealousy has mutated into specific sexual logistics, and his moral outrage has settled on Baldwin's apparent passivity. 'That lazy bastard' is one of the episode's most quotable lines — it tells you everything about Larry Sanders in four words.

dialogue.speaker: Alec
dialogue.line: Hey, call me Lar.

jokes.text: Hank pitching the restaurant to Alec Baldwin as an investor during the commercial break — 'So, as an investor, you'd be making the restaurant go around. Me, I'm just the symbol. I'm just the face on the menu.'
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to recruit investors for his rotating restaurant; he's cornered Baldwin during the break
jokes.punchline: 'I'm just the face on the menu' — Hank reduces himself to a logo in his own vision, which somehow makes the pitch more grandiose, not less
jokes.explanation: A solid Hank delusion beat. The image of Hank as 'the face on the menu' of a street-level rotating restaurant with no view is an absurdly small ambition dressed in celebrity branding language. The comedy is in how sincerely he offers himself as a minor symbol.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The people around The country are going, 'He's staying.'

jokes.text: Baldwin's response to the restaurant pitch: 'I'd have to talk to my business manager.' / Hank: 'Oh come on. Those guys don't know jack shit.'
jokes.setup: Baldwin gives the polite brush-off of consulting his business manager
jokes.punchline: Hank dismisses business managers entirely — while being in a meeting that arose precisely because his own business manager shot down his plan
jokes.explanation: Excellent irony — Hank is literally in this situation because his own business manager was right, yet he dismisses all business managers as clueless. Classic sitcom dramatic irony delivered with crisp economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Alec dated my ex-wife Francine.

jokes.text: 'What color is my tie?' / 'Blue.' / 'That part is. That's the part I was looking at.'
jokes.setup: Artie wants to pull Baldwin from the show; Larry wants to prove he's calm and professional
jokes.punchline: Larry's bizarre 'What color is my tie?' test — and his response to Artie's correct answer — is a non-sequitur logic that only a person unraveling would find reassuring
jokes.explanation: A small gem. Larry's 'sanity test' via tie color is itself irrational — knowing what color your tie is proves nothing about emotional stability. 'That part is. That's the part I was looking at.' implies Larry needs a very localized version of reality to be correct and that's enough for him. High quotability, excellent character integration — this is Larry's magical thinking made comic.

dialogue.speaker: Alec
dialogue.line: I was referring to our charity work with multiple sclerosis.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I know. I know. That, too.

jokes.text: Ed Begley Jr. announces 'No, I mean I dated Francine also.' — straight to camera, in the middle of the MS charity discussion
jokes.setup: The show returns from commercial; Larry is steering toward charity discussion to avoid the Francine subject
jokes.punchline: Ed Begley wades directly into the Francine conversation — unprompted, cheerfully — adding himself to the list
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the Francine running gag reaches its perfect second act here. The audience has been conditioned to expect a specific kind of embarrassment; Ed Begley Jr. adding himself to the list is both surprising and inevitable. The comedy of Begley — a mild-mannered environmentalist actor — as a Francine conquest is perfectly cast.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: From the time he walked out all I saw was him fucking her. And she was on top. That lazy bastard.

jokes.text: 'I met her at one of my roller-skating parties.' / Larry: 'Ed, Francine was my date at the roller-skating party.' / 'The sign on the wall said all skate.'
jokes.setup: Ed reveals he met Francine at a roller-skating party — Larry was also there, with Francine
jokes.punchline: 'The sign on the wall said all skate' — Ed's airtight legal defense for poaching your date is that the rink's open-skate policy constitutes permission for all activities
jokes.explanation: Arguably the single funniest joke in the episode. 'The sign on the wall said all skate' is a perfect punchline — completely unexpected, internally logical in the most absurd way, and infinitely quotable. The comedy works on multiple levels: Ed is genuinely offering this as a satisfactory explanation; the reductive equivalence of a rink policy to a permission slip for seduction is inspired. The economy is flawless: five words carry enormous comic weight. This is 9-level joke writing.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Those guys don't know jack shit.

jokes.text: 'So you did it on wheels?' — audience member/Larry's response to Ed's roller-skating admission
jokes.setup: 'The sign said all skate' implies whatever happened at the roller rink
jokes.punchline: The audience/Larry connecting the skating context to the sexual implication — 'on wheels' — causes the crowd to erupt
jokes.explanation: The follow-up laugh after 'all skate.' Not as elegant — it spells out the implication rather than leaving it — but gets a big reaction because the audience is already primed and happy. The punchline does its job.

dialogue.speaker: Ed Begley Jr.
dialogue.line: I dated Francine also.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Has anybody else been with my ex-wife?' — delivered to the entire studio audience
jokes.setup: The Francine list has now grown to include two on-air guests
jokes.punchline: Larry throws open the question to the whole room — resigned, deadpan, completely defeated
jokes.explanation: Excellent line reading moment. Larry's resignation — turning his personal catastrophe into an open-floor audience participation segment — is perfectly Larry Sanders. The economy is excellent: nine words of total defeat. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ed Begley Jr.
dialogue.line: I met her at one of my roller-skating parties.

jokes.text: "Has anybody else been with my ex-wife?" — Larry, to the entire studio audience.
jokes.setup: Two guests have now revealed they dated Francine. Larry addresses the room.
jokes.punchline: The question is delivered with genuine exhaustion — Larry has lost control of his own show and is now polling the audience. The implicit answer (yes, obviously) makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: A great escalation beat — Larry's defeated query to the studio audience is the comedic acknowledgment that the situation has completely escaped his control. The economy is perfect: one question does all the work. Strong moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ed Begley Jr.
dialogue.line: The sign on the wall said 'all skate.' It means anybody can do whatever they want.

jokes.text: 'How about the guy who plays the piano with his ass?'
jokes.setup: Larry has opened the floor to anyone who's slept with Francine
jokes.punchline: Larry himself invokes the armless piano player — who has been a running in-joke — as a potential Francine conquest, then turns off the TV in disgust
jokes.explanation: A perfect multi-callback that ties together the armless pianist running gag and the Francine list. Larry turning off the TV immediately after is an implied visual reaction beat — he can't even finish the thought. The economy of the callback is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: So you did it on wheels?

jokes.text: "How about the guy who plays the piano with his ass?" — a staff member suggesting the armless pianist also dated Francine.
jokes.setup: Larry has just asked if anyone else has been with his ex-wife.
jokes.punchline: The armless pianist, who has been a recurring background joke, is now implied as another of Francine's conquests — Larry immediately turns off the TV.
jokes.explanation: The armless pianist callback pays off perfectly — he's been a background running gag and now enters the Francine mythology. Larry turning off the television is the visual button. Good structural comedy that rewards viewers who tracked the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Has anybody else been with my ex-wife?

jokes.text: The long sigh and silence after Larry turns off the TV — Francine watching the broadcast
jokes.setup: Francine has been watching the show where her entire sexual history was just broadcast
jokes.punchline: The sigh and silence is the joke — there is no verbal response adequate to this situation
jokes.explanation: A necessary tonal beat — the silence after the broadcast chaos grounds us in Francine's perspective. Not a big laugh but a real one, earned by the absurdity of the situation.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: How about the guy who plays the piano with his ass?

jokes.text: 'What are the odds that you would have slept with the same three people on one show in one night?' — Larry's bewildered accounting
jokes.setup: Francine confronts Larry about broadcasting her history; Larry is trying to process the statistical improbability
jokes.punchline: Larry reframes the catastrophe as an extraordinary coincidence — 'three people on one show in one night' — as if the problem is logistical rather than personal
jokes.explanation: Larry doing math on his humiliation is very on-brand. The comedy is in how he approaches a personal crisis as a logistical puzzle — it's deflection dressed up as bewilderment.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: It was like a theme show. Who's the third?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Me. That would be me. I would be the third.

jokes.text: 'Three? ... Me. That would be me. I would be the third.' / 'I didn't realize you were counting the host.'
jokes.setup: Larry says three people; Francine asks who the third is
jokes.punchline: Larry — counting himself, Alec Baldwin, and Ed Begley Jr. — has to clarify that he is the third; Francine's 'I didn't realize you were counting the host' treats Larry as just another name on a list
jokes.explanation: Francine's line is a minor devastation — Larry has grouped himself with his romantic rivals as just 'the host,' and she confirms it. Excellent character moment. 'I didn't realize you were counting the host' has strong quotability because it perfectly captures a specific kind of romantic diminishment.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: I didn't sleep with Ed Begley or the man who plays the piano with his ass!

jokes.text: 'It was like a theme show.'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to describe the surreal experience of interviewing two of his ex-wife's lovers on the same night
jokes.punchline: 'Theme show' — Larry's instinct is to categorize his personal nightmare as a programming concept
jokes.explanation: Two words of perfect Larry Sanders: his compulsive tendency to view everything through the lens of television production. 'Theme show' reframes his humiliation as content. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Legitimate acts Of penetration... Oral sex... And I think Heavy petting, don't you?

jokes.text: 'I didn't sleep with Ed Begley or the man who plays the piano with his ass!'
jokes.setup: Francine is defending her honor after Larry's show made her seem like she slept with everyone
jokes.punchline: Her specific list of denials — including the piano player — invokes the running gag one more time and confirms the armless pianist has become the episode's absurdist anchor
jokes.explanation: The armless pianist callback gets its funniest use here — Francine's urgent denial ('the man who plays the piano with his ass') dignifies the joke by treating it as a real allegation requiring denial. The character integration is good: only someone truly defensive would include this in their list.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: If you keep narrowing it down like this, I'm not going to have any names on my list.

jokes.text: "My God, maybe I should just make you a list of everybody I've ever slept with." / "You know what? Maybe you should."
jokes.setup: Francine makes what she thinks is an outrageous suggestion in frustration.
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately and sincerely takes her up on it — 'That's not a bad idea.' The bluff is called.
jokes.explanation: The setup for the episode's B-plot engine (the lists) is well-constructed. Larry's immediate acceptance of a clearly rhetorical offer reveals both his jealousy and his passive-aggressive nature — he frames it as perfectly reasonable.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: You could throw your wrist out.

jokes.text: 'Maybe I should just make you a list of everybody I've ever slept with.' / 'You know what? Maybe you should.' ... 'And, uh, I'll be wanting a list from you.' / 'That's a different thing.'
jokes.setup: The argument about exes has escalated to a mutual transparency proposal
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately agrees to the list exchange, then when Francine asks for his list in return — 'That's a different thing.' The double standard lands instantly.
jokes.explanation: A very well-structured character joke. The beat from 'maybe you should' to 'that's a different thing' is efficient and true — Larry's self-awareness about his double standard arrives in the same breath as the double standard. Perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Making my Christmas card list.

jokes.text: Larry narrows the list criteria down: 'Legitimate acts of penetration... oral sex... and I think heavy petting, don't you?' / 'If you keep narrowing it down like this, I'm not going to have any names on my list.'
jokes.setup: Larry is defining the scope of the list
jokes.punchline: Francine's response reveals that Larry's 'sexual history' apparently requires very specific definitions to populate — implying his list is going to be short and sad
jokes.explanation: A great double-edged joke. Larry's lawyerly categorization of sexual activities is funny on its own (the clinical distance from intimacy is very Larry). But Francine's punchline reframes it as a tacit admission that his list needs these categories to have any entries. The self-undermining quality is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That's a big mistake.

jokes.text: Larry defining parameters for his list: "Legitimate acts of penetration... oral sex... and I think heavy petting, don't you?" / "If you keep narrowing it down like this, I'm not going to have any names on my list."
jokes.setup: Larry is establishing the categories for what counts on a sexual history list.
jokes.punchline: Francine's response — 'If you keep narrowing it down, I won't have any names' — is the punchline, but it's the legal-precision with which Larry applies criteria (as if these are contract terms) that makes it funny.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation — Larry applying bureaucratic precision to intimacy reveals his controlling nature, and Francine's response is both self-aware and a counter-dig at Larry's experience level. The rhythm of 'legitimate acts of penetration... oral sex... heavy petting, don't you?' builds well.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: You mean Rebecca Arthur.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Why?

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Yeah.

jokes.text: Larry writing the list furiously and Francine telling him 'You shouldn't write so fast. You're going to pull something. You could throw your wrist out.'
jokes.setup: Larry has committed to the list and is writing intensely
jokes.punchline: Francine's mock-concern about Larry injuring his wrist while compiling his sexual history is lightly cruel — the implication being that if he's writing this fast, something is wrong
jokes.explanation: A functional visual/character beat. The humor comes from the image of Larry writing furiously (either the list is surprisingly long, or he's compensating with speed) and Francine's dry concern. Not a major laugh but earns its moment.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: 'Adrienne Barbeau'! Why, you no-good, star-screwing bastard! Get the hell out of here!

jokes.text: Artie visits after the show; Larry claims he and his wife didn't watch the broadcast. Artie: 'Horseshit. She's already got you lying to your friends again.'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to downplay the catastrophic broadcast; Artie sees through it instantly
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'horseshit' and immediate diagnosis — 'she's already got you lying to your friends again' — identifies a pattern Artie has watched play out in Larry's relationships before
jokes.explanation: Artie in father-figure mode, which is always excellent. 'She's already got you lying to your friends again' does real character work — it implies this is a documented pattern, not a one-time incident. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: There must be 85 to 100 names.

jokes.text: Artie hovering over what he claims is his 'Christmas card list'
jokes.setup: Artie has clearly been working on something when Larry walks in; he deflects when asked
jokes.punchline: 'Making my Christmas card list' — delivered with a straight face in what is clearly not December, and clearly not a Christmas card list
jokes.explanation: A small dry comedy beat — Artie's nonchalant deflection implies he was doing something embarrassing (possibly making his own list, or tracking the Francine situation). The deadpan delivery is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You're making a mistake. A big, big mistake.

jokes.text: Larry asking his staffer who 'Balki's girlfriend' is on Perfect Strangers — cross-referencing her for his sex list
jokes.setup: Larry is working on his list; he needs to identify specific women by TV character name
jokes.punchline: That Larry's sexual history is catalogued in his brain by TV character rather than real name reveals the depth of his showbiz-brain pathology
jokes.explanation: An inspired character detail. Only a late-night talk show host would organize his sexual past by the TV shows women appeared in. It's funny, sad, and deeply revealing about Larry's world. 'Balki's girlfriend' is the perfect specific detail — not a major star, but definitively a TV person.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: I can't believe it took six years for you to find out!

jokes.text: "People discuss it, but nobody actually makes the list."
jokes.setup: Larry has told a staff member about the list exchange with Francine.
jokes.punchline: The staffer's assessment — everyone talks about doing this, nobody actually does it — functions as a precise observation about the gap between relationship confrontation bravado and reality.
jokes.explanation: A good observational line that functions as both character insight and social commentary. Not a big joke but contributes to the episode's thematic throughline. 'Nobody actually makes the list' is a truth everyone recognizes.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I've been really busy.

jokes.text: The staffer role-plays as Francine reading Larry's list: 'Adrienne Barbeau!' followed by shrieking 'Why, you no-good, star-screwing bastard!'
jokes.setup: The staffer offers to show Larry how a woman would react to his list; he takes the list and role-plays Francine
jokes.punchline: 'Star-screwing bastard!' — the staffer's Francine reaction instantly jumps to maximum hysteria at just the first name
jokes.explanation: Strong comedy beat. 'Star-screwing bastard' is a great insult because it's specific to the world of the show — not just an infidelity insult but one that identifies the TYPE of infidelity (celebrity-chasing). The instant escalation from first name to nuclear reaction is funny and well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Francine
dialogue.line: Does the restaurant have a big crank outside? That's kind of inconvenient, you rush outside every time you want the floor to turn?

jokes.text: Artie arrives at Larry's house to find the Francine list situation. His reaction to the two-page, 85-100 name list: 'Jesus Christ, that's hefty. It's a two-pager at least.'
jokes.setup: Larry explains Francine gave him a list; Artie assumes it's a joke or a sketch
jokes.punchline: 'That's hefty. It's a two-pager at least.' — Artie's measured, almost professional assessment of the list's length is funnier than any exclamation of shock
jokes.explanation: Artie's tone — almost like an editor reviewing a manuscript — is perfectly calibrated. 'Two-pager at least' treats Francine's sexual history like a policy brief. The deadpan quantification (85-100 names) is funnier than any wider reaction would be.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Which, by the way, is not a piece-of-shit Saab, I might say.

jokes.text: 'I'm not going to look at it.' — Larry refusing to read Francine's list, immediately after being told there are 85-100 names
jokes.setup: The list exists; Artie says 'You're making a mistake'
jokes.punchline: Larry's instant, firm refusal — after earlier demanding the list — reveals that having it is enough; looking at it would be too real
jokes.explanation: A good character beat — Larry's avoidance of the very information he insisted on is deeply human and funny. The callback to his earlier insistence makes the refusal land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Which, by the way, Is not a piece-of-shit saab, I might say.

jokes.text: Artie's entrance upon seeing Francine: 'Francine, what a delight to see you, my dear. We've all missed you. You've done something with your hair.' / 'I cut it shorter.' / 'You're looking well yourself.' / 'How's, uh...' / 'She's just doing wonderfully. I'll send her your regards.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just been briefed on the entire Francine situation; she arrives at the door
jokes.punchline: Artie performs a flawless society greeting — 'what a delight,' 'we've all missed you' — despite having just been describing her as a disaster. Then he and Francine seamlessly complete each other's awkward social sentence about his wife.
jokes.explanation: An excellent piece of Hollywood social comedy. Artie's instantaneous pivot from 'that woman smashed your award' to 'what a delight to see you' is pure showbiz. The collaborative completion of the awkward 'How's your wife' question (both Artie and Francine navigate it gracefully) shows these are people trained in the performance of niceness. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Daniel Baldwin
dialogue.line: I've never considered it a charity, but I used to do your ex-wife.

jokes.text: Artie exits with 'If you don't mind, excuse me. I have a paycheck to earn.' — allowing the awkward reunion
jokes.setup: Larry and Francine need to talk privately; Artie needs to make an exit
jokes.punchline: Artie's excuse — 'I have a paycheck to earn' — is funny in its mundane professionalism; he's been managing this situation all episode and now bills it as just doing his job
jokes.explanation: A clean Artie exit line. The idea that all of this — managing Larry's romantic catastrophes, reviewing Francine's list — is just 'earning a paycheck' is a wry summation of a producer's life.

jokes.text: Francine: 'He hasn't changed a bit.' Larry: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just performed his flawless social exit
jokes.punchline: Both Larry and Francine agree that Artie is exactly the same as he's always been — the beat is warm and observational, and both characters share a moment of genuine affection for the chaos
jokes.explanation: A small, warm beat. Not a big laugh but a genuine moment — two people who've known each other a long time sharing a quiet understanding. Functions as a tonal reset.

jokes.text: 'I'm a human shredder.' — Larry offering to destroy both lists by hand-tearing
jokes.setup: Larry and Francine agree to rip up the lists; Larry makes the ceremonial offer
jokes.punchline: 'I'm a human shredder' — Larry's self-designation is both grandiose and pathetic; he's turned list destruction into a performance
jokes.explanation: A good small Larry line — the self-branding instinct ('I'm a human shredder') kicking in during what should be an intimate moment. Four words that compress his entire showbiz personality.

jokes.text: After the cathartic list-tearing, Francine: 'I want the ones you screwed while we were married. I'm making a collage.'
jokes.setup: The list-tearing has been established as a healing, moving-on moment
jokes.punchline: Francine immediately pivots from reconciliation to revenge art — 'I'm making a collage' reframes the torn paper as craft supplies for an art project about his infidelities
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structural misdirection is perfect: the list-tearing ritual has been framed as closure, but Francine's 'I'm making a collage' instantly recontextualizes it as the beginning of revenge. The word 'collage' is specifically, brilliantly chosen — it's the most passive-aggressive, art-school-adjacent way to describe cataloguing your ex-husband's infidelities. Economy is flawless. This is genuinely excellent comedic writing.

jokes.text: Larry and Francine's moment of reconnection is immediately undercut by Francine's admission: 'I realize that the only reason I went out with Alec and Ed was because I wanted to hurt you.' / 'I can't believe it took six years for you to find out!'
jokes.setup: Francine is making a genuine emotional admission about her motivations
jokes.punchline: Larry's outrage is not about the betrayal itself, but that it took him six years to learn about it — the wounded pride of a paranoid man who missed the obvious
jokes.explanation: A perfectly character-integrated laugh. A normal person's reaction to 'I dated your rivals to hurt you' would be hurt or anger about the betrayal. Larry's reaction — 'I can't believe it took SIX YEARS' — is the reaction of a man whose primary wound is that his intelligence was underestimated. This is Larry Sanders at his most nakedly Larry.

jokes.text: 'I've been really busy.' — Larry's response to why he didn't figure out Francine's intentions sooner
jokes.setup: 'I can't believe it took six years to find out' — Larry is outraged he missed the obvious
jokes.punchline: Larry's excuse — 'I've been really busy' — is the most inadequate, showbiz-self-absorbed explanation for six years of emotional obliviousness
jokes.explanation: Four words that perfectly encapsulate Larry Sanders the character. 'I've been really busy' explains his entire emotional life. The economy is near-perfect — maximum character revelation per syllable. Strong quotability because it's universal in the worst way.

jokes.text: Hank barging in with restaurant pitch materials at the worst possible moment: 'At Hank's Look-Around Cafe... spins, so will your head, as you receive your profit statements!'
jokes.setup: Larry and Francine are in the middle of a fragile, genuine emotional reconnection
jokes.punchline: Hank's total obliviousness to the emotional temperature of the room — bursting in with investment pitch materials — is a perfect comic interruption
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom intrusion comedy elevated by character specificity. Hank's timing is terrible, but his sales pitch ('so will your head, as you receive your profit statements') is also terrible on its own terms. The joke works because Hank is constitutionally unable to read a room.

jokes.text: Francine: 'Did I hurt you?' / Larry: 'Really hurt me.' / Francine: 'Good.'
jokes.setup: Francine is asking about the emotional impact of her revenge plan.
jokes.punchline: Larry's confirmation that he was hurt, followed by Francine's satisfied 'Good' — presented as a tender exchange.
jokes.explanation: The exchange works as both sweet and twisted — there's genuine intimacy in the confirmation that the hurt was real and effective. Francine's 'Good' is delicious: satisfied, warm, and slightly sociopathic all at once. Economy is the joke's main virtue.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Does the restaurant have a big crank outside? That's kind of inconvenient — you rush outside every time you want the floor to turn?'
jokes.setup: Hank is pitching the rotating restaurant; Francine interrupts with a practical question
jokes.punchline: The image of restaurant patrons rushing outside to manually crank the floor is the most vivid summation yet of the fundamental impracticality of Hank's entire concept
jokes.explanation: A good escalation of the restaurant absurdity. The specificity of 'rushing outside to crank the floor' between bites is a funny image that exposes the whole concept's fundamental silliness.

jokes.text: Hank: 'And the name Hank — that's not set in stone.'
jokes.setup: Hank is being pushed out of the room; his whole restaurant pitch is collapsing
jokes.punchline: Hank's final concession — the name itself is negotiable — reveals that he has no fixed point in this plan except the rotating floor (which is also unfinanceable). Everything is provisional except the gimmick.
jokes.explanation: A perfect small Hank line. 'That's not set in stone' about his own name on his own restaurant concept is the sound of a man negotiating from a position of total weakness while believing he's being magnanimous. Economy is excellent — seven words tell us everything about Hank's delusional salesmanship.

jokes.text: 'He's probably built this on his own. That's the sad part.'
jokes.setup: Hank has left behind elaborate restaurant pitch materials
jokes.punchline: Larry's quiet, sympathetic observation — that Hank constructed all these promotional materials himself — briefly humanizes the absurdity
jokes.explanation: A good tonal shift — the comedy of Hank's delusion briefly acquires a shade of pathos. 'That's the sad part' has the Larry Sanders quality of being genuinely funny and quietly devastating simultaneously. The rewatch bonus is for appreciating the emotional complexity of the observation.

jokes.text: Larry and Francine referencing 'that time in the car' as one of their five dates — 'which, by the way, is not a piece-of-shit Saab'
jokes.setup: They're taking stock of their new relationship — 'only four dates, five if you count that time in the car'
jokes.punchline: Larry defensively notes his car is not a 'piece-of-shit Saab' — a callback to Francine's earlier jab about Alec Baldwin's Saab, but now applied defensively to Larry's own car
jokes.explanation: A well-earned callback that closes the loop on the Saab detail established early. Larry's defensiveness about his own car while using Alec Baldwin's as a put-down earlier reveals his competitive anxiety. The 'time in the car' euphemism is also a nicely understated beat.

jokes.text: "Five if you count that time in the car. Which, by the way, is not a piece-of-shit SAAB, I might say."
jokes.setup: Larry and Francine are assessing how quickly they're moving in their renewed relationship.
jokes.punchline: Francine casually defends Larry's car against the implied criticism — calling back Alec Baldwin's SAAB (which Larry asked about earlier) and distinguishing Larry's car from it.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback — the SAAB returns as a motif, and Francine's defensive 'not a piece-of-shit SAAB' implies she knows Larry was thinking of Baldwin's car all along. The callback rewards attentive viewers and adds a layer to the Larry/Alec rivalry.

jokes.text: 'If things go well, you can ream me out later.' / 'It'll be my pleasure.' / 'Really?' / 'Yeah.' / 'OK. I look forward to that.'
jokes.setup: They're agreeing to take things slow; Larry makes a self-deprecating offer
jokes.punchline: Francine's 'it'll be my pleasure' — a sincere acknowledgment that she will, in fact, enjoy reaming him out — and Larry's delighted surprise ('Really?') lands as both romantic and darkly funny
jokes.explanation: A good closing beat for the Larry-Francine arc. The comedy is in the twisted dynamic being established: both parties understand that confrontation is a form of intimacy for them. Larry's 'OK. I look forward to that' is the perfect Larry beat — masochistic anticipation.

jokes.text: Daniel Baldwin: 'You and I have something in common.' / Larry: 'Evidently you're speaking of the charity work—' / Daniel: 'No, no, no. I've never considered it a charity, but I used to do your ex-wife.'
jokes.setup: The exact same comedic structure as the Alec Baldwin interview (Joke 27) — 'something in common' setup — but now with a third Baldwin and a more explicit punchline
jokes.punchline: 'I've never considered it a charity, but I used to do your ex-wife.' — Daniel's phrasing ('I've never considered it a charity') is a twisted wordplay on the charity framework Larry tried to deploy, plus the escalation to 'do' is more explicit than anything said before
jokes.explanation: The episode's final joke and a structural masterpiece. The show reuses the exact same setup ('you and I have something in common') — which now functions as a known pattern the audience anticipates — and then subverts it again with a variation. Daniel's 'I've never considered it a charity' is a brilliant extra twist: it takes the MS charity framework that's been running all episode and weaponizes it as wordplay. The escalation from Alec to Ed to Daniel Baldwin completes the arc perfectly. Larry cutting immediately to the clip without comment is the perfect button.

jokes.text: Larry's immediate redirect to the clip: 'All right, so you brought a clip from Homicide? Let's get right to the clip. You don't need to set it up. No, really — we're good. We're doing the clip.'
jokes.setup: Daniel Baldwin has just announced he slept with Francine on live television
jokes.punchline: Larry's rapid-fire clip escalation — interrupting any further elaboration — is both a professional television reflex and a survival mechanism. The repetition ('we're good. We're doing the clip.') signals total collapse of Larry's composure
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the episode's comedy engine. Larry's panicked over-directing of the clip roll is exactly right — the professional mask is back on but barely holding. 'We're good. We're doing the clip.' is the sound of a man using television production as a shield. Excellent character integration and structure as a closing beat.

tmdb_overview: A chance remark by Francine leads Larry to ask for a list of all her sexual partners since their divorce.
